title: Dix-Hallpike Test
purpose: Gold-standard positional test for posterior semicircular canal BPPV.
structure: Posterior semicircular canal (canalithiasis); vestibulo-ocular reflex producing nystagmus.
procedure: Patient in long-sitting with a pillow placed so the head will extend 20 degrees when lying back. Stand on the side to be tested and hold the head firmly in 45 degrees rotation towards that side (aligns the posterior canal with the sagittal plane). Patient keeps the eyes open; move the patient quickly backwards so the head stays rotated and extended 20 degrees. Observe latency, duration and direction of nystagmus (latency usually 5-20 s, fatigues within 60 s). After vertigo and nystagmus resolve, slowly sit the patient up (reverse nystagmus may appear). If negative, repeat on the other side.
positive: Vertigo with upbeating torsional nystagmus (upper pole of the eye beating towards the dependent ear, vertical component towards the forehead) = posterior canal BPPV. Lateral-beating or downbeating nystagmus suggests lateral or anterior canal BPPV; negative on both sides with suspected BPPV = test the lateral canal with the supine head roll test.

accuracy.source: none; regarded as the gold standard, so no external reference standard for accuracy data (Bhattacharyya et al. 2017 BPPV guideline)

notes: Source: high clinical value as the best available test. Anterior canal BPPV is rare (1-3%) and should be referred to a specialist. Companion tests: supine head roll test, head impulse test.

title: Supine Head Roll Test
purpose: Diagnose lateral (horizontal) semicircular canal BPPV (also Pagnini-Lempert or Pagnini-McClure roll test).
structure: Lateral semicircular canal (5-22% of BPPV cases); canalithiasis in the long arm or near the ampulla.
procedure: Indicated when the history fits BPPV and the Dix-Hallpike shows only horizontal or no nystagmus; warn the patient that vertigo and nausea may occur (bucket at hand). Patient supine, head flexed 30 degrees (lateral canal horizontal). Quickly rotate the head 90 degrees to one side and watch for nystagmus (latency 5-20 s, fatigues within 60 s); return to face-up; after any nystagmus subsides, quickly turn 90 degrees to the other side and observe again.
positive: Vertigo with predominantly horizontal nystagmus. Geotropic type: intense nystagmus beating towards the ground on the affected side, weaker on the healthy side (debris in the long arm). Apogeotropic type (less common): nystagmus beating towards the uppermost ear on both sides (debris adherent or near the ampulla); the affected ear is opposite the stronger nystagmus.
notes: About 20% of BPPV resolves within 4 weeks and up to 50% within 3 months untreated; recurrence 10-18% after 1 year; lateral canal BPPV self-resolves faster than posterior. Companion tests: Dix-Hallpike, head impulse test.

title: Epley Maneuver
purpose: Treatment: modified Epley canalith repositioning manoeuvre for posterior canal BPPV.
structure: Posterior semicircular canal (85-95% of BPPV cases).
procedure: Start as in a positive Dix-Hallpike: long-sitting with a pillow for 20 degrees extension, head rotated 45 degrees to the affected (here right) side. Quickly lie the patient back with the head still rotated and extended; hold 20-30 s. Quickly turn the head 90 degrees to the unaffected side; hold 20 s. Patient rolls onto the left shoulder and turns the head a further 90 degrees so the face points down at 45 degrees; hold 20-30 s. Sit the patient up. Left side is the exact mirror.
positive: n/a (treatment). Warn about vertigo and nausea (17-32%); check the patient tolerates neck movement.

accuracy.source: n/a (treatment). Hilton & Pinder 2014 Cochrane review: more effective than sham/control, no difference vs Semont, success up to 80%

notes: Treatment page, not a diagnostic test. Post-manoeuvre restrictions are unnecessary (Devaiah & Andreoli 2010 meta-analysis). Repeat sessions help persistent nystagmus. Canal conversion posterior to lateral occurs in 6-7% of repositioning procedures. Alternatives: Semont (posterior), BBQ roll (lateral).

title: Semont Maneuver
purpose: Treatment: Semont liberatory manoeuvre for posterior canal BPPV.
structure: Posterior semicircular canal (85-95% of BPPV cases).
procedure: Patient sits in the middle of the bench with the head turned away from the affected (right) side. Quickly bring the patient into side-lying towards the affected side with the head turned up; nystagmus and vertigo follow shortly; hold until at least 20 s after nystagmus stops (some recommend 1-2 min). Quickly move the patient up and through sitting into the opposite side-lying with the head facing down, keeping the same head position; hold about 30 s (some authors 2-10 min). Slowly sit the patient up.
positive: n/a (treatment). Warn about vertigo and nausea; check neck movement tolerance.

accuracy.source: n/a (treatment). Hilton & Pinder 2014 Cochrane review: more effective than sham/control, no difference vs Epley, success up to 85%

notes: Treatment page, not a diagnostic test. ⚠ The nausea sentence on this page reads 'the Epley maneuver can lead to nausea ... 17-32%' (copied from the Epley page). Post-manoeuvre restrictions unnecessary (Devaiah 2010); repeat sessions help persistent nystagmus; canal conversion 6-7%. Alternatives: Epley (posterior), BBQ roll (lateral).

title: BBQ Roll Maneuver
purpose: Treatment: barbecue (360-degree) roll manoeuvre for geotropic lateral canal BPPV.
structure: Lateral semicircular canal (debris in the long arm).
procedure: Diagnose the affected side first with the supine head roll test. Patient supine; some authors start with the head rolled towards the affected (right) side, held 15-30 s or until nystagmus stops. Roll the head to the unaffected side, hold 15-30 s. Keep rolling in the same direction until the patient is prone, nose down, 15-30 s (some end here and sit the patient up). Originally the roll continues to 360 degrees onto the right side, 15-30 s, then sit up.
positive: n/a (treatment). Warn about vertigo and nausea; check neck movement tolerance.

accuracy.source: n/a (treatment). Cohort studies and case reports: success 50-100%; Kim et al. 2012: better than sham at 1 h and 1 month

notes: Treatment page, not a diagnostic test. ⚠ The page's background text says canalithiasis affects the posterior canal in 85-95% (copied from the posterior-canal pages) although the manoeuvre targets the lateral canal. Kim 2012 is cited in text but not in the reference list. Post-manoeuvre restrictions unnecessary (Devaiah 2010). Alternatives for posterior BPPV: Epley, Semont.

title: Head Impulse Test
purpose: Bedside test to distinguish peripheral (vestibular neuronitis) from central (cerebellar/brainstem stroke) causes of prolonged vertigo.
structure: Vestibulo-ocular reflex of the tested side (horizontal semicircular canal / vestibular nerve).
procedure: Only in prolonged vertigo (brief episodes suggest BPPV: use Dix-Hallpike). Examiner sits in front of the patient with a hand on each side of the head; patient fixates the examiner's nose and keeps the eyes open even if vertigo worsens. Quickly turn the head towards the tested side while watching the eyes; slowly return to neutral; repeat several times.
positive: A corrective (catch-up) saccade back to the target after the impulse indicates peripheral vestibular loss on that side (Weber et al. 2008; the page itself does not spell out the criterion).

accuracy.source: Dros et al. 2010 (CMAJ), analysis of 7 studies

notes: Source: high clinical value to confirm peripheral vestibular dysfunction in prolonged dizziness. ⚠ The page describes the procedure but not what counts as positive; the catch-up saccade criterion is from the listed Weber 2008 reference. Molnar & McGee 2014 also listed.

title: Cervical Torsion Test
purpose: Provoke dizziness/nystagmus by neck torsion (trunk rotation under a fixed head) to support cervicogenic dizziness.
structure: Cervical afferents isolated by rotating the trunk while the head stays still; cervico-ocular reflex.
procedure: Patient on a swivel chair, hips and knees 90 degrees, eyes closed. Fixate the head in neutral; patient actively rotates the trunk to one side at least 45 and up to 90 degrees and holds 30 s (four positions in the full protocol).
positive: Dizziness, visual disturbance, unusual eye movements on opening the eyes, speech disturbance, motion sickness or nausea, slurred speech, dysphagia, light-headedness, tinnitus, headache or paraesthesia during any position or immediately after.

accuracy.sensitivity: not reported (not yet evaluated in symptomatic groups)
accuracy.source: Treleaven et al. (text 2019, reference 2020, Phys Ther); L'Heureux-Lebeau et al. 2014 reported strong utility vs BPPV

notes: Source: clinical use unknown until sensitivity is evaluated. Nystagmus may occur in healthy people via the cervico-ocular reflex and is hard to see without video-oculography, so subjective symptoms are used. ⚠ Treleaven cited as 2019 in text, 2020 in the reference list; author spelled 'Trealeaven'.

title: Head-Neck Differentiation Test
purpose: Differentiate cervicogenic dizziness by rhythmic trunk rotation under a fixed head.
structure: Cervical afferents (neck torsion without vestibular stimulation).
procedure: Patient on a swivel chair, eyes closed, hips and knees 90 degrees. Fixate the head in neutral; patient actively rotates the trunk left and right 45 degrees using the legs at a metronome pace of 60 beats per minute.
positive: Dizziness, visual disturbance, unusual eye movements after opening the eyes, speech disturbance, motion sickness or nausea, slurred speech, dysphagia, light-headedness, tinnitus, headache or paraesthesia during or immediately after.

accuracy.sensitivity: not reported (not yet evaluated in symptomatic groups)
accuracy.source: Treleaven et al. (text 2019, reference 2020, Phys Ther)

notes: Source: clinical use unknown at this moment. ⚠ Treleaven cited as 2019 in text, 2020 in the reference list; author spelled 'Trealeaven'. Companion: cervical torsion test, smooth pursuit neck torsion test.

title: Smooth Pursuit Neck Torsion Test
purpose: Detect disturbed eye-movement control from abnormal cervical afferent input (cervicogenic dizziness, traumatic neck pain).
structure: Cervical proprioception influencing smooth-pursuit eye movements.
procedure: Patient sits on a swivel stool, head horizontal and kept steady; the chair is turned to bring 45 degrees of neck torsion. Patient follows a slowly moving target with the eyes horizontally right and left. Done in neutral, trunk turned right and trunk turned left.
positive: Clinically: dizziness reproduced in the torsion position compared with neutral. In the laboratory the outcome is the velocity of corrective saccades (needs instruments).

accuracy.source: Tjell 1998 (Am J Otol), traumatic neck pain with dizziness vs vertigo/CNS/Meniere/healthy; only study

notes: Source: moderate clinical value because of the single study.

title: Joint Position Sense Error
purpose: Measure cervical proprioception: accuracy of returning the head to a target after a neck movement (JPSE).
structure: Cervical proprioception; whiplash patients with dizziness show larger errors (Treleaven 2003); traumatic neck pain shows larger JPSE than controls (de Vries 2015 review).
procedure: Patient sitting with a head-mounted laser pointing at a target about 90 cm (3 feet) away. Eyes closed, turn the head fully to the right, then relocate to the start; measure the distance from the start point. Open eyes, recentre, close eyes, repeat for at least 6 trials. Repeat for left rotation, flexion and extension. Move slowly: faster movement reflects vestibular rather than cervical afference.
positive: Mean error over 4.5 degrees in any direction (over 6 cm on this target, i.e. at least half the dots outside the second ring).

accuracy.source: n/a (measurement). Reliability: Roren et al. 2009, test-retest ICC 0.68 (laser method)

notes: In non-traumatic neck pain only half of the studies show enlarged JPSE.

title: Gaze Stability
purpose: Assess the ability to keep the gaze on a target while the head moves (sensorimotor control in traumatic neck pain / cervicogenic dizziness).
structure: Eye-movement control under cervical afferent input.
procedure: Patient sitting keeps the eyes on a fixed target while actively rotating the head right, then left, then flexing and extending. Watch one eye at a time.
positive: Inability to keep focus, over- or undershooting, reduced or awkward cervical motion, or dizziness, blurred vision or nausea.
notes: Part of the dizziness exam battery with saccades, eye-head coordination, postural stability, JPSE and the neck torsion tests.

title: Saccadic Eye Movement
purpose: Assess rapid eye movements that change the point of fixation (sensorimotor control in neck disorders).
procedure: Patient sitting, head neutral and still. Option 1: follow a target about 1 m away that is moved quickly and held still, in several directions. Option 2: two targets at eye level 1 m away and 30 cm apart; look from one to the other as quickly as possible. Several repetitions; watch one eye at a time.
positive: Inability to keep focus on the target, over- or undershooting, or dizziness, blurred vision or nausea.
notes: Part of the dizziness exam battery.

title: Eye-Head Coordination
purpose: Assess the ability to maintain gaze while both eyes and head move (sensorimotor control in neck disorders).
structure: Eye-head coordination under cervical afferent input.
procedure: Patient sitting, head neutral. Two targets at eye level about 1 m away and 30 cm apart, horizontally and then vertically. Patient moves eyes and head in the same direction to focus on a target, eyes leading, then the head, keeping the eyes on the target.
positive: Inability to keep focus, over- or undershooting, reduced or awkward cervical motion, or dizziness, blurred vision or nausea.
notes: Part of the dizziness exam battery.

title: Postural Stability
purpose: Modified sensory organisation test for postural stability deficits in traumatic neck pain and cervicogenic dizziness.
structure: Postural control relying on vision and somatosensory input when cervical afferent input is disturbed.
procedure: Barefoot, arms across the chest with hands on the shoulders, each 30 s. Narrow stance: feet together, ankle bones touching; progress to a foam mat of about 10 cm with eyes open, then eyes closed. Tandem stance: progress with eyes closed. Single-leg stance: free leg flexed and not touching; progress with eyes closed.
positive: Unable to hold 30 s, large increase in sway, slow correction of sway, or rigidity to prevent sway. Healthy under 60 should hold narrow-stance tests 30 s; healthy under 45 should also complete tandem and single-leg tests.

accuracy.source: n/a (performance test). Treleaven et al. 2005 (CTSIB): traumatic neck pain with dizziness showed greater sway and more failures than without dizziness and controls

notes: Part of the dizziness exam battery.
